bibl.title: Rapid Tuning of Auditory “What” and “Where” Pathways by Training

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether improvement in the first hour of training is task familiarisation or a real change in what the perceptual system is tuned to
span.quote: Behavioral improvement within the first hour of training is commonly explained as procedural learning (i.e., strategy changes resulting from task familiarization). However, it may additionally reflect a rapid adjustment of the perceptual and/or attentional system in a goal-directed task.

span.label: whether 45 minutes of training on one acoustic cue produces gains and brain activity specific to that cue rather than general to the task
span.quote: One important issue that has not been fully analyzed or confirmed is the specificity of the neuroplastic changes observed during these early stages of learning. Although animal studies have provided evidence for rapid adjustment of the perceptual system during training (for a review see Fritz et al. 2005a ), it remains to be determined whether such feature-specific effects take place in humans. In human studies, the nonspecific behavioral improvement observed in the early stages of learning (i.e., lack of specificity) is often taken as evidence for procedural learning with feature-specific effects emerging only after multiple daily training sessions ( Watson 1980 ; Karni and Bertini 1997 ). Although there is some behavioral evidence for specificity within the first training session ( Hawkey et al. 2004 ; Hussain et al. 2012 ), neurophysiological evidence supporting such feature-specific effects is lacking.

span.label: a double dissociation in which listeners trained on pitch or on location gain specifically from that cue and recruit ventral or dorsal areas respectively, with the stimuli identical across groups
span.quote: More importantly, the contrast between the 2 groups revealed a striking double dissociation in which listeners trained on spectral or spatial cues showed higher source activity in ventral (“what”) and dorsal (“where”) brain areas, respectively.

span.label: existence
span.quote: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a feature-specific gain in human brain activity following a brief training designed to enhance perceptual sensitivity to differences in voice pitch and voice location.

span.label: rapid feature-specific auditory perceptual learning
span.quote: In the present study, we investigated whether a brief 45-min training program can yield a rapid feature-specific modulation on both behavior and neuromagnetic activity during subsequent measurement while participants identified 2 vowels presented simultaneously.

span.label: meg
span.quote: MEG data were recorded in a magnetically shielded room using a 151-channel whole-head neuromagnetometer (VSM Medtech, Port Coquitlam, BC, Canada).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the training session acts as a priming episode that biases top-down attention toward the trained acoustic cue, so that cue is processed as more salient in the later untrained test
span.quote: In the present study, the training phase may act as a priming task that biased attention toward the trained acoustic feature even when, in the subsequent task, participants were not explicitly told to focus attention on the voice or location.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the implicit attentional bias makes the trained spectral or spatial difference more salient than the untrained one, which differentially recruits the ventral or dorsal auditory stream
span.quote: That is, the training may implicitly bias participants to focus their attention on the trained spectral or location difference between the 2 vowels, which would appear more salient than the untrained cue during MEG measurement that followed the brief training session.

span.label: training may act as a priming task that biases attention to the trained cue, making it more salient later even without instruction
span.quote: In the present study, the training phase may act as a priming task that biased attention toward the trained acoustic feature even when, in the subsequent task, participants were not explicitly told to focus attention on the voice or location. That is, the training may implicitly bias participants to focus their attention on the trained spectral or location difference between the 2 vowels, which would appear more salient than the untrained cue during MEG measurement that followed the brief training session.

span.label: the selectivity survives the delay to the MEG session and the absence of feedback there
span.quote: This training-induced selectivity appears to be fairly long-lasting and resilient, as it lingers throughout the delay between training and MEG recording and remains even when participants did not receive feedback on their performance during the MEG session.

span.label: training changes how the two cues combine, not just how well each is used
span.quote: However, here in both trained groups, the gain from the trained cue was almost as large as having both cues simultaneously, which was only slightly higher than that from the trained cue alone (both t 11 > 2.80, P < 0.05). Moreover, the sum of gains from each cue was considerably larger than having both cues simultaneously

span.label: the animal precedent is that receptive fields shift within minutes of a task, and much less when the same sounds are heard passively
span.quote: For instance, changes in the receptive fields of ferret auditory cortex can occur within minutes of a tone discrimination task that was previously learned ( Fritz et al. 2003 , 2005a , 2005b ). However, these neuroplastic changes were smaller or absent if the animal listened passively to the same sounds (i.e., when the sounds are task-irrelevant).

span.label: A repetition/familiarity effect cannot be fully excluded as a partial cause of the behavioural and neural changes.
span.quote: Although the pattern of behavioral and neuromagnetic data appears to be consistent with an attention bias and/or changes in perceptual sensitivity, it remains possible that changes in performance and brain activity can be partially due to a repetition effect.

span.label: The study cannot say whether these rapid source-activity changes are precursors of longer-term plasticity; that needs combined MEG and fMRI work.
span.quote: Further research combining both MEG and fMRI may help clarify the neural interactions underlying such rapid neuroplastic changes, which could help determine whether these rapid changes in source activity are precursors to long-term changes as the training regimen continues.

span.label: the dissociation is a bias in recruitment rather than an all-or-none separation of the two streams
span.quote: Notably, this group difference was not all or none, but rather appeared to reflect a bias in recruiting ventral or dorsal brain regions while performing the double-vowel identification task. This is consistent with prior fMRI studies that have revealed relative differences in activation in auditory “what” and “where” processing streams as a function of task instruction/demand and selective attention effect rather than absolute differences

span.label: the untrained comparison group comes from a previous study rather than being run alongside these two
span.quote: Notably, we have previously shown that, in a group performing the same task on the same set of stimuli without pre-MEG training, the benefit from either the Δƒ 0 or Δlocation cue did not differ from one another and that from having access to both cues equaled the sum of gains for each single cue

span.label: the frequency group's gain for the trained one-semitone cue did not improve across training blocks, unlike the location group's
span.quote: For the Frequency group, participants' gain in accuracy for the 1-semitone Δƒ 0 did not differ between blocks 1 and 4 ( t 11 = 1.28, P = 0.23). For the Location group, participants achieved a significantly higher gain in accuracy for the 90° separation in blocks 2–4 compared with block 1 (all t 11 > 2.20, P < 0.05, paired t -tests), indicating improved cue utilization after training.

span.label: repetition priming remains a possible partial contributor, which the paper argues against rather than excludes
span.quote: Although the pattern of behavioral and neuromagnetic data appears to be consistent with an attention bias and/or changes in perceptual sensitivity, it remains possible that changes in performance and brain activity can be partially due to a repetition effect. Evidence from a repetition priming paradigm has shown superior performance in identifying auditory stimuli when the same stimuli were used in a prior task ( Stuart and Jones 1995 ). Consequently, in the Frequency and Location groups, the enhanced performance for Δƒ 0 and Δlocation, respectively, could be attributed to the fact that the participants were more familiar with the stimuli.

span.label: the what and where stream division, applied to audition
span.quote: acoustic features well known to stimulate distinct ventral (“what”) and dorsal (“where”) neural pathways in humans

span.label: HRTFs, used to render spatial separation over headphones
span.quote: The HRTF coefficients were individually determined by a brief sound localization task at the beginning of the experiment. On each trial, 1 of the 4 vowels was presented at 1 of the 5 azimuth locations (i.e., −90°, −45°, 0°, 45°, 90°) using a variety of HRTF coefficients selected from the TDT library that best suited the participant's head size. Participants were asked to point toward the sound source location. The HRTF coefficient that resulted in the most accurate localization responses was then determined and used for the remainder of the experiment for each participant.

span.label: the finding that task relevance, not exposure, drives rapid receptive-field change
span.quote: For instance, changes in the receptive fields of ferret auditory cortex can occur within minutes of a tone discrimination task that was previously learned ( Fritz et al. 2003 , 2005a , 2005b ). However, these neuroplastic changes were smaller or absent if the animal listened passively to the same sounds (i.e., when the sounds are task-irrelevant).

span.label: the first training block, before any training, compared between the two groups at the 0-semitone / 0-degree baseline
span.quote: Both the Frequency and Location groups achieved about 40% accuracy (the chance level is 25%) under the baseline condition (when the 2 vowels had 0-semitone difference in Δƒ 0 and 0° spatial separation) in the first block of the training session, indicating no remarkable group difference before training.

span.label: comparison against participants trained on the OTHER feature and against an untrained group from an earlier study
span.quote: In addition, in both trained groups, the gain in accuracy for the trained feature was greater than that observed in participants trained on the other feature or a control group ( Du et al. 2011 ) who was not exposed to nor trained on the same stimuli prior to the MEG recording session.

span.label: analysing the GAIN attributable to frequency or spatial separation rather than raw accuracy
span.quote: That is, the analyses focused on the gain related to having frequency or spatial separation, and this approach controlled for having the same stimuli present in the training and the MEG recording session.

span.label: double dissociation here means a RELATIVE bias in recruitment, not categorical separation - the paper says the group difference was not all or none
span.quote: Notably, this group difference was not all or none, but rather appeared to reflect a bias in recruiting ventral or dorsal brain regions while performing the double-vowel identification task. This is consistent with prior fMRI studies that have revealed relative differences in activation in auditory “what” and “where” processing streams as a function of task instruction/demand and selective attention effect rather than absolute differences

span.label: the gain measure is always a DIFFERENCE from the same-pitch same-location baseline, which is what makes it independent of stimulus familiarity
span.quote: However, this explanation is unlikely for 2 reasons. First, the SFSL condition was also presented during both training and MEG recording, but there was little evidence of repetition priming for this trial type. More importantly, the feature-specific effects observed in the present study reflect a relative rather than an absolute difference between the training and the MEG recording. That is, the analyses focused on the gain related to having frequency or spatial separation, and this approach controlled for having the same stimuli present in the training and the MEG recording session.

span.label: spatial separation is simulated over headphones by a HRTF chosen per participant, so location is a rendered cue rather than a physical one
span.quote: The HRTF coefficients were individually determined by a brief sound localization task at the beginning of the experiment. On each trial, 1 of the 4 vowels was presented at 1 of the 5 azimuth locations (i.e., −90°, −45°, 0°, 45°, 90°) using a variety of HRTF coefficients selected from the TDT library that best suited the participant's head size. Participants were asked to point toward the sound source location. The HRTF coefficient that resulted in the most accurate localization responses was then determined and used for the remainder of the experiment for each participant.

span.label: feature-specific learning is contrasted throughout with procedural learning, defined as strategy change from task familiarisation
span.quote: Behavioral improvement within the first hour of training is commonly explained as procedural learning (i.e., strategy changes resulting from task familiarization). However, it may additionally reflect a rapid adjustment of the perceptual and/or attentional system in a goal-directed task.

span.label: the ventral and dorsal streams are imported as established what and where pathways, and the paper's dissociation is read against that prior assignment rather than establishing it
span.quote: acoustic features well known to stimulate distinct ventral (“what”) and dorsal (“where”) neural pathways in humans

span.label: builds-on → Du et al. 2011
span.quote: Notably, we have previously shown that, in a group performing the same task on the same set of stimuli without pre-MEG training, the benefit from either the Δƒ 0 or Δlocation cue did not differ from one another and that from having access to both cues equaled the sum of gains for each single cue ( Du et al. 2011 ).

span.label: extends → Alain et al. 2007; Alain, Campeanu, et al. 2010; Ben-David et al. 2011; Spierer et al. 2007
span.quote: Our findings provide further evidence for rapid changes in cortical evoked responses after less than an hour of auditory training on sound spectro-temporal ( Alain et al. 2007 ; Alain, Campeanu, et al. 2010 ; Ben-David et al. 2011 ) or spatial ( Spierer et al. 2007 ) features, and offer the first neuroimaging evidence for rapid perceptual (i.e., feature-specific) learning in humans.

span.label: contradicts → the view that first-hour improvement is procedural learning without feature specificity
span.quote: If the rapid improvement reflects primarily procedural learning that is independent of trained features, one would anticipate that the training effects on behavioral and neuromagnetic data would be comparable between the differentially trained groups. On the other hand, if learning does involve a rapid adjustment in perceptual sensitivity to the task-relevant attribute, then one would predict feature-specific gains in performance. That is, participants that receive spectral training should perform better when a Δƒ 0 cue is available relative to when a Δlocation cue is present, and vice versa.

span.label: extends → behavioural reports of within-session specificity, by supplying the neurophysiological evidence they lacked
span.note: status: the paper's own words: remains to be determined
span.quote: One important issue that has not been fully analyzed or confirmed is the specificity of the neuroplastic changes observed during these early stages of learning. Although animal studies have provided evidence for rapid adjustment of the perceptual system during training (for a review see Fritz et al. 2005a ), it remains to be determined whether such feature-specific effects take place in humans. In human studies, the nonspecific behavioral improvement observed in the early stages of learning (i.e., lack of specificity) is often taken as evidence for procedural learning with feature-specific effects emerging only after multiple daily training sessions ( Watson 1980 ; Karni and Bertini 1997 ). Although there is some behavioral evidence for specificity within the first training session ( Hawkey et al. 2004 ; Hussain et al. 2012 ), neurophysiological evidence supporting such feature-specific effects is lacking.

span.label: confirms → animal work showing receptive fields change within minutes of a task and much less during passive listening
span.quote: For instance, changes in the receptive fields of ferret auditory cortex can occur within minutes of a tone discrimination task that was previously learned ( Fritz et al. 2003 , 2005a , 2005b ). However, these neuroplastic changes were smaller or absent if the animal listened passively to the same sounds (i.e., when the sounds are task-irrelevant).

span.label: builds-on → Du et al. 2011, whose untrained group supplies the additivity baseline
span.quote: Notably, we have previously shown that, in a group performing the same task on the same set of stimuli without pre-MEG training, the benefit from either the Δƒ 0 or Δlocation cue did not differ from one another and that from having access to both cues equaled the sum of gains for each single cue

span.label: supports → the ventral what and dorsal where division of auditory cortical processing
span.quote: Thus, although both groups were processing the same set of stimuli, distinct brain networks were revealed depending on the trained features, with the Frequency group recruiting more anterior and ventral temporo-frontal areas (“what” pathway) while the Location group activating more posterior and dorsal temporo-parietal areas (“where” pathway).

span.label: procedural learning —distinct-from→ perceptual sensitivity
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION, stated in advance: procedural learning predicts comparable effects across differently trained groups, perceptual change predicts feature-specific gains. The rival is given its own prediction
span.quote: If the rapid improvement reflects primarily procedural learning that is independent of trained features, one would anticipate that the training effects on behavioral and neuromagnetic data would be comparable between the differentially trained groups. On the other hand, if learning does involve a rapid adjustment in perceptual sensitivity to the task-relevant attribute, then one would predict feature-specific gains in performance. That is, participants that receive spectral training should perform better when a Δƒ 0 cue is available relative to when a Δlocation cue is present, and vice versa.

span.label: ventral —contrasted-with→ dorsal
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — SCOPED: the paper calls the group difference a bias in recruitment and not all or none, so the weight is deliberately below 1
span.quote: Notably, this group difference was not all or none, but rather appeared to reflect a bias in recruiting ventral or dorsal brain regions while performing the double-vowel identification task. This is consistent with prior fMRI studies that have revealed relative differences in activation in auditory “what” and “where” processing streams as a function of task instruction/demand and selective attention effect rather than absolute differences

span.label: IFG —part-of→ ventral
span.quote: Compared with the Location group, the Frequency group showed larger source activity in the bilateral IFG (right IFG, 80–120 and 230–270 ms intervals; left IFG, 280–370 ms interval), the left STG (130–220 ms interval), the left middle temporal gyrus (MTG, 180–220 ms interval), and bilateral prG (right prG, 130–170 ms interval; left prG, 280–320 ms interval).

span.label: IPL —part-of→ dorsal
span.quote: In comparison, the Location group exhibited larger source activity than the Frequency group in more posterior and dorsal areas, namely, the right supramarginal gyrus (SMG, 30–70, 230–270 and 330–370 ms intervals), the bilateral IPL (right IPL, 80–120 and 280–320 ms intervals; left IPL, 130–170 and 230–270 ms intervals), the left angular gyrus (AG, 130–170 ms interval), the left MTG (180–220 ms interval), the posterior area of the left STG (230–270 ms interval), the right prG (230–270 ms interval), the right poG (280–320 ms interval), and the right middle frontal gyrus (280–320 ms interval).

span.label: gain in accuracy —distinct-from→ repetition priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — CRITERION: the measure is a difference from a baseline present in both phases, so stimulus familiarity cancels
span.quote: However, this explanation is unlikely for 2 reasons. First, the SFSL condition was also presented during both training and MEG recording, but there was little evidence of repetition priming for this trial type. More importantly, the feature-specific effects observed in the present study reflect a relative rather than an absolute difference between the training and the MEG recording. That is, the analyses focused on the gain related to having frequency or spatial separation, and this approach controlled for having the same stimuli present in the training and the MEG recording session.

span.label: HRTF —operationalised-as→ dorsal
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — the spatial cue is rendered per participant by a filter chosen from a localisation task, not a real source position
span.quote: The HRTF coefficients were individually determined by a brief sound localization task at the beginning of the experiment. On each trial, 1 of the 4 vowels was presented at 1 of the 5 azimuth locations (i.e., −90°, −45°, 0°, 45°, 90°) using a variety of HRTF coefficients selected from the TDT library that best suited the participant's head size. Participants were asked to point toward the sound source location. The HRTF coefficient that resulted in the most accurate localization responses was then determined and used for the remainder of the experiment for each participant.

span.label: attention —causes→ perceptual sensitivity
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — the paper offers attentional bias as the route and does not separate it from a change in sensitivity
span.quote: In the present study, the training phase may act as a priming task that biased attention toward the trained acoustic feature even when, in the subsequent task, participants were not explicitly told to focus attention on the voice or location. That is, the training may implicitly bias participants to focus their attention on the trained spectral or location difference between the 2 vowels, which would appear more salient than the untrained cue during MEG measurement that followed the brief training session.

span.label: concurrent-vowel —operationalised-as→ gain in accuracy
span.quote: Participants in the Frequency group showed a greater gain in performance for Δƒ 0 alone than for Δlocation alone ( t 11 = 6.06, P < 0.001). Conversely, participants in the Location group showed a greater gain for Δlocation alone than for Δƒ 0 alone ( t 11 = 2.38, P = 0.036).

span.label: receptive fields —operationalised-as→ perceptual sensitivity
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — the animal precedent measures the same idea one level down, in single-neuron tuning rather than in performance
span.quote: For instance, changes in the receptive fields of ferret auditory cortex can occur within minutes of a tone discrimination task that was previously learned ( Fritz et al. 2003 , 2005a , 2005b ). However, these neuroplastic changes were smaller or absent if the animal listened passively to the same sounds (i.e., when the sounds are task-irrelevant).

span.label: MEG —part-of→ ER-SAM
span.quote: It reveals that performance during the double-vowel task was associated with a widely distributed neural network. More specifically, we found significant activity in bilateral auditory cortices that started in Heschl's gyrus, the location of primary auditory cortex, around 88 ms, and extended into the STG and insula by 250 ms.

span.label: semitone —operationalised-as→ ventral
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — the pitch cue is graded in semitones from 0 to 4, the location cue in degrees - two scales that cannot be equated, so the two training regimes are matched in structure and not in difficulty
span.quote: For the Frequency group, each vowel pair contained 1 vowel with ƒ 0 at 100 Hz and the other ƒ 0 at 100, 103, 106, 112, or 126 Hz, resulting in 5 levels of Δƒ 0 : 0, 0.5, 1, 2, or 4 semitones. Both vowels were presented from the midline.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by 1-way ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests, and t -tests were conducted for behavioral data with the null-hypothesis rejection level set at 0.05.

span.label: post hoc test
span.quote: Repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by 1-way ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests, and t -tests were conducted for behavioral data with the null-hypothesis rejection level set at 0.05.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: First, a voxel-wise, mixed-effect 2-factor ANOVA with group as the fixed factor and with participant as the random factor was computed for each epoch using the 3dANOVA2 function in AFNI.

span.label: Monte Carlo simulation (multiple-comparison correction)
span.quote: To correct for multiple comparisons, a spatial cluster extent threshold was applied by using AlphaSim with 4096 (2 12 ) Monte Carlo simulations.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The 2 regions were chosen as showing a significant (corrected P < 0.05) group difference in source activity. ** P < 0.01 by Pearson correlation.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: The error bars represent the standard error of the mean.

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: In both groups, a repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of block ( F 3,33 = 37.30 and 15.02, respectively, P < 0.001 in both cases), indicating improved vowel accuracy with practice.

span.label: paired t -tests
span.quote: For the Frequency group, participants' gain in accuracy for the 1-semitone Δƒ 0 did not differ between blocks 1 and 4 ( t 11 = 1.28, P = 0.23). For the Location group, participants achieved a significantly higher gain in accuracy for the 90° separation in blocks 2–4 compared with block 1 (all t 11 > 2.20, P < 0.05, paired t -tests), indicating improved cue utilization after training.

span.label: Pearson correlation
span.quote: As shown by Figure 4 A , individuals' mean source activity in the right IFG during the 80–120 ms interval significantly correlated with listeners' gain in accuracy for Δƒ 0 cue alone ( R 2 = 0.58, P < 0.01, Pearson correlation). Participants from the Frequency and Location groups nicely formed 2 clusters with the former showing a larger gain in performance by Δƒ 0 cue and stronger source activity in the right IFG than the latter.

span.label: family-wise corrected
span.quote: All activations were significant at family-wise corrected P < 0.05 with the cluster size no smaller than 1088 μL.

span.label: Groups trained on a spectral versus a spatial cue showed a double dissociation in brain activity, ventral areas for the spectral group and dorsal areas for the spatial group, despite identical stimuli.
span.quote: More importantly, the contrast between the 2 groups revealed a striking double dissociation in which listeners trained on spectral or spatial cues showed higher source activity in ventral (“what”) and dorsal (“where”) brain areas, respectively.

span.label: Behavioural benefit after training was specific to the trained acoustic feature rather than general.
span.quote: Participants in the Frequency group showed a greater gain in performance for Δƒ 0 alone than for Δlocation alone ( t 11 = 6.06, P < 0.001).

span.label: The group difference in cortical source activity appeared within roughly 100 ms of sound onset, which the authors read as a pre-stimulus attentional bias toward the trained feature.
span.quote: Notably, the group difference in the ventral and dorsal stream activity began as early as 100 ms after sound onset, suggesting the preset (before the presentation of stimuli) attentional bias on trained attributes and differential “warm-up” of corresponding pathways.

span.label: Because both groups faced identical stimulus-response demands, the difference cannot be explained as procedural learning.
span.quote: These group differences reflect a rapid recalibration of the perceptual system with training and cannot be easily accounted for by procedural learning, because the stimulus-response requirements were identical in both groups.

span.label: After training the two cues no longer combined additively: the trained cue alone captured almost all of the benefit available from both cues together.
span.quote: Moreover, the sum of gains from each cue was considerably larger than having both cues simultaneously (both t 11 > 5.80, P < 0.01, paired t -tests).

span.label: The two groups improved equally with practice overall, so the feature-specific effect is not an artefact of one group simply learning more.
span.quote: However, the interaction between group and block was not significant ( F 3,33 = 1.17, P = 0.34), nor was the 3-way interaction between group, block, and level of difference between the 2 vowels ( F 12,132 = 0.56, P = 0.87), indicating equal gains in accuracy from practice in both groups and for all levels of Δƒ 0 and Δlocation.

span.label: The authors claim priority for showing feature-specific plasticity in human brain activity after under an hour of training.
span.quote: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a feature-specific gain in human brain activity following a brief training designed to enhance perceptual sensitivity to differences in voice pitch and voice location.

span.label: both groups improved with practice during the training session
span.quote: In both groups, a repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of block ( F 3,33 = 37.30 and 15.02, respectively, P < 0.001 in both cases), indicating improved vowel accuracy with practice.

span.label: the frequency-trained group gained more from a pitch difference and the location-trained group more from a spatial difference
span.quote: Participants in the Frequency group showed a greater gain in performance for Δƒ 0 alone than for Δlocation alone ( t 11 = 6.06, P < 0.001). Conversely, participants in the Location group showed a greater gain for Δlocation alone than for Δƒ 0 alone ( t 11 = 2.38, P = 0.036).

span.label: the group by trial-type interaction was large and each group beat the other on its own trained cue
span.quote: A mixed-model, repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between group and trial type ( F 2,44 = 33.32, P < 0.001). The Frequency group exhibited a higher gain from Δƒ 0 alone than the Location group ( t 22 = 4.17, P < 0.001), whereas the Location group showed a greater gain from Δlocation alone than the Frequency group ( t 22 = 6.18, P < 0.001). There was no significant group difference when the 2 vowels differed in both ƒ 0 and location.

span.label: no group difference remained when both cues were available at once
span.quote: A mixed-model, repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between group and trial type ( F 2,44 = 33.32, P < 0.001). The Frequency group exhibited a higher gain from Δƒ 0 alone than the Location group ( t 22 = 4.17, P < 0.001), whereas the Location group showed a greater gain from Δlocation alone than the Frequency group ( t 22 = 6.18, P < 0.001). There was no significant group difference when the 2 vowels differed in both ƒ 0 and location.

span.label: the frequency-trained group recruited inferior frontal and temporal areas more strongly
span.quote: Compared with the Location group, the Frequency group showed larger source activity in the bilateral IFG (right IFG, 80–120 and 230–270 ms intervals; left IFG, 280–370 ms interval), the left STG (130–220 ms interval), the left middle temporal gyrus (MTG, 180–220 ms interval), and bilateral prG (right prG, 130–170 ms interval; left prG, 280–320 ms interval).

span.label: the location-trained group recruited parietal and posterior temporal areas more strongly
span.quote: In comparison, the Location group exhibited larger source activity than the Frequency group in more posterior and dorsal areas, namely, the right supramarginal gyrus (SMG, 30–70, 230–270 and 330–370 ms intervals), the bilateral IPL (right IPL, 80–120 and 280–320 ms intervals; left IPL, 130–170 and 230–270 ms intervals), the left angular gyrus (AG, 130–170 ms interval), the left MTG (180–220 ms interval), the posterior area of the left STG (230–270 ms interval), the right prG (230–270 ms interval), the right poG (280–320 ms interval), and the right middle frontal gyrus (280–320 ms interval).

span.label: the two networks differed although both groups heard exactly the same stimuli
span.quote: Thus, although both groups were processing the same set of stimuli, distinct brain networks were revealed depending on the trained features, with the Frequency group recruiting more anterior and ventral temporo-frontal areas (“what” pathway) while the Location group activating more posterior and dorsal temporo-parietal areas (“where” pathway).

span.label: right inferior frontal activity at 80-120 ms correlated with individual gain from the pitch cue
span.quote: As shown by Figure 4 A , individuals' mean source activity in the right IFG during the 80–120 ms interval significantly correlated with listeners' gain in accuracy for Δƒ 0 cue alone ( R 2 = 0.58, P < 0.01, Pearson correlation). Participants from the Frequency and Location groups nicely formed 2 clusters with the former showing a larger gain in performance by Δƒ 0 cue and stronger source activity in the right IFG than the latter.

span.label: STRUCTURAL CHANGE: untrained listeners gain additively from the two cues, whereas trained listeners gain almost as much from the trained cue alone as from both
span.quote: However, here in both trained groups, the gain from the trained cue was almost as large as having both cues simultaneously, which was only slightly higher than that from the trained cue alone (both t 11 > 2.80, P < 0.05). Moreover, the sum of gains from each cue was considerably larger than having both cues simultaneously

span.label: CONTROL NULL: no group by block interaction, so both groups improved equally overall and the specificity is not one group learning more
span.quote: The Location group displayed a smaller overall improvement in performance than the Frequency group during training, which may suggest different learning curves for spectral and spatial training. However, the interaction between group and block was not significant ( F 3,33 = 1.17, P = 0.34), nor was the 3-way interaction between group, block, and level of difference between the 2 vowels ( F 12,132 = 0.56, P = 0.87), indicating equal gains in accuracy from practice in both groups and for all levels of

span.label: CONTROL: the same-pitch same-location condition appeared in both phases and showed little repetition priming
span.quote: However, this explanation is unlikely for 2 reasons. First, the SFSL condition was also presented during both training and MEG recording, but there was little evidence of repetition priming for this trial type. More importantly, the feature-specific effects observed in the present study reflect a relative rather than an absolute difference between the training and the MEG recording. That is, the analyses focused on the gain related to having frequency or spatial separation, and this approach controlled for having the same stimuli present in the training and the MEG recording session.

span.label: ASYMMETRY: across training blocks the location group improved its use of the trained cue while the frequency group did not
span.quote: For the Frequency group, participants' gain in accuracy for the 1-semitone Δƒ 0 did not differ between blocks 1 and 4 ( t 11 = 1.28, P = 0.23). For the Location group, participants achieved a significantly higher gain in accuracy for the 90° separation in blocks 2–4 compared with block 1 (all t 11 > 2.20, P < 0.05, paired t -tests), indicating improved cue utilization after training.

span.label: SCOPE STATED: the group difference is a bias in recruitment rather than an all-or-none separation
span.quote: Notably, this group difference was not all or none, but rather appeared to reflect a bias in recruiting ventral or dorsal brain regions while performing the double-vowel identification task. This is consistent with prior fMRI studies that have revealed relative differences in activation in auditory “what” and “where” processing streams as a function of task instruction/demand and selective attention effect rather than absolute differences

span.label: procedural learning
span.quote: These rapid changes in behavioral performance were previously thought to solely reflect procedural learning, that is, changes in participants' strategies that occurred during task familiarization ( Karni and Bertini 1997 ; Karni et al. 1998 ; Wright and Fitzgerald 2001 ).

span.label: SFSL / SFDL / DFSL / DFDL trial types
span.term: SFSL / SFDL / DFSL / DFDL trial types
span.quote: These 4 trial types were labeled as follows: same ƒ 0 same location (SFSL), same ƒ 0 different location (SFDL), different ƒ 0 same location (DFSL), and different ƒ 0 different location (DFDL), and were randomized and balanced in 4 blocks of 144 trials.

span.label: synthetic aperture magnetometry (SAM)
span.quote: The synthetic aperture magnetometry (SAM), a minimum-variance beamformer algorithm ( Van Veen et al. 1997 ), was used as a spatial filter to estimate the time course of source activity on a lattice of 5-mm spacing across the whole-brain volume in the 0.3 to 20 Hz frequency range.

span.label: procedural learning
span.quote: Behavioral improvement within the first hour of training is commonly explained as procedural learning (i.e., strategy changes resulting from task familiarization). However, it may additionally reflect a rapid adjustment of the perceptual and/or attentional system in a goal-directed task.

span.label: HRTF
span.quote: The HRTF coefficients were individually determined by a brief sound localization task at the beginning of the experiment. On each trial, 1 of the 4 vowels was presented at 1 of the 5 azimuth locations (i.e., −90°, −45°, 0°, 45°, 90°) using a variety of HRTF coefficients selected from the TDT library that best suited the participant's head size. Participants were asked to point toward the sound source location. The HRTF coefficient that resulted in the most accurate localization responses was then determined and used for the remainder of the experiment for each participant.

span.label: double dissociation
span.quote: More importantly, the contrast between the 2 groups revealed a striking double dissociation in which listeners trained on spectral or spatial cues showed higher source activity in ventral (“what”) and dorsal (“where”) brain areas, respectively.

span.label: training group (spectral Frequency training vs spatial Location training)
span.term: training group (spectral Frequency training vs spatial Location training)
span.quote: Twenty-four participants who provided written informed consent according to the University of Toronto and Baycrest Hospital Human Subject Review Committee guidelines were randomly assigned into 2 training groups: the Frequency group (7 women; aged 20–33 years; mean: 24 years) and the Location group (8 women; aged 20–31 years; mean: 24 years).

span.label: trial type: presence of a fundamental-frequency difference and/or a spatial-location difference between the two vowels

span.quote: Participants were presented with 4 trial types, which were created by the orthogonal combination of Δƒ 0 and Δlocation.

span.label: accuracy of identifying both concurrent vowels
span.term: accuracy of identifying both concurrent vowels
span.quote: Their task was to identify both vowels by sequentially pressing corresponding keys on the keyboard.

span.label: MEG cortical source activity (normalized pseudo-Z)
span.quote: The time course of source activity at each node/voxel was estimated as a weighted linear combination of the magnetic field measured at all MEG sensors and represented as a normalized pseudo- Z measure ( Robinson and Vrba 1998 ).

span.label: bottom-up sensory input (identical stimulus set across groups)
span.term: bottom-up sensory input (identical stimulus set across groups)
span.quote: This procedure enabled us to investigate the behavioral and neuroplastic changes induced by training listeners to use either spectral or spatial cues in speech separation and identification while holding the bottom-up sensory input constant.

span.label: gain in accuracy
span.quote: Participants in the Frequency group showed a greater gain in performance for Δƒ 0 alone than for Δlocation alone ( t 11 = 6.06, P < 0.001). Conversely, participants in the Location group showed a greater gain for Δlocation alone than for Δƒ 0 alone ( t 11 = 2.38, P = 0.036).

span.label: semitone
span.quote: For the Frequency group, each vowel pair contained 1 vowel with ƒ 0 at 100 Hz and the other ƒ 0 at 100, 103, 106, 112, or 126 Hz, resulting in 5 levels of Δƒ 0 : 0, 0.5, 1, 2, or 4 semitones. Both vowels were presented from the midline.

span.label: MEG
span.quote: It reveals that performance during the double-vowel task was associated with a widely distributed neural network. More specifically, we found significant activity in bilateral auditory cortices that started in Heschl's gyrus, the location of primary auditory cortex, around 88 ms, and extended into the STG and insula by 250 ms.

span.label: R 2 = 0.58 — variance shared between right inferior frontal gyrus source activity at 80-120 ms and the behavioural gain from the pitch cue
span.quote: R 2 = 0.58, P < 0.01, Pearson correlation). Participants from the Frequency and Location groups nicely formed 2 clusters with the former showing a larger gain in performance by Δƒ 0 cue and stronger source activity in the right IFG than the latter.

span.label: about 40% accuracy (chance 25%) — baseline double-vowel identification accuracy of both groups in the first training block

span.label: t 22 = 4.17, P < 0.001 / t 22 = 6.18, P < 0.001 — between-group tests confirming each group benefited more than the other from its own trained cue
span.quote: The Frequency group exhibited a higher gain from Δƒ 0 alone than the Location group ( t 22 = 4.17, P < 0.001), whereas the Location group showed a greater gain from Δlocation alone than the Frequency group ( t 22 = 6.18, P < 0.001).

span.label: F 2,44 = 33.32, P < 0.001 — group-by-trial-type interaction, the statistical core of the feature-specific behavioural effect
span.quote: A mixed-model, repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between group and trial type ( F 2,44 = 33.32, P < 0.001).

span.quote: Each vowel was presented individually (16 trials, 4 vowels by 2 ƒ 0 levels, 100 and 106 Hz), and participants identified the vowel by pressing 1 of 4 keys on the keyboard, marked “AH,” “ER,” “EE,” and “OO.” All participants achieved single vowel accuracy of 95% or better.
